questions.stem: What creates the molecular ion in a mass spectrometer?

options.text: A high-energy electron beam knocks one electron out of the molecule
options.explanation: Bombardment removes one electron from the pair, leaving a positive ion with an unpaired electron.

options.text: The molecule captures an extra electron from the beam
options.explanation: Capturing would make a negative ion; mass spectrometry of organics makes positive ions.

options.text: The molecule is heated until it ionises spontaneously
options.explanation: Ionisation comes from electron bombardment, not from heating alone.

options.text: A magnet strips electrons from the molecule before detection
options.explanation: The magnet deflects existing ions; it does not ionise them.

questions.stem: A doubly charged ion of mass 16 arrives at the detector. Its m/z value is

options.explanation: That divides by 4, a charge the ion does not carry.
m/z divides mass by charge: 16 / 2 = 8.
That ignores the 2+ charge, which halves the ratio.
That multiplies instead of divides, reversing the ratio's meaning.

questions.stem: Which ions are deflected the most on the way to the detector?

options.text: Neutral fragments formed during fragmentation
options.explanation: Neutral species are not accelerated or deflected; they are not detected at all.

options.text: Ions attracted to the positive pole of the magnet
options.explanation: Positive ions are pulled towards the negative pole.

options.text: The smaller and more positively charged fragments
options.explanation: Deflection grows as mass falls and as charge rises, so light, highly charged ions bend hardest.

options.text: The heaviest singly charged ions
options.explanation: Heavy ions resist deflection and bend least.

questions.stem: What does the tallest peak of a mass spectrum represent?

options.text: The molecular ion, always the last peak
options.explanation: The molecular ion is the highest m/z peak, not necessarily the tallest.

options.text: The fragment with the largest m/z value
options.explanation: Largest m/z is the molecular ion region, unrelated to abundance.

options.text: An artefact of detector noise
options.explanation: The base peak is a real signal from the dominant ion.

options.text: The most abundant ion, giving the tallest peak
options.explanation: Abundance sets peak height, and the tallest peak is called the base peak.

questions.stem: After fragmentation, the charged fragments are separated inside the spectrometer by

options.text: Their mass-to-charge ratio as they deflect in the magnetic field
options.explanation: The field bends each ion's path by an amount set by mass and charge, so m/z sorts the fragments.

options.text: Their colour when excited by the electron beam
options.explanation: No optical sorting happens in a mass spectrometer.

options.text: Their speed through the sample inlet
options.explanation: The inlet does not separate anything; separation happens after acceleration.

options.text: Their boiling points under vacuum
options.explanation: Boiling point is irrelevant to ion sorting.

questions.stem: Define the molecular ion of a compound in mass spectrometry.
questions.modelAnswer: The molecular ion is the whole molecule with one electron removed by the electron beam, carrying a positive charge and giving the peak at the highest m/z.

questions.stem: State what is meant by the m/z value of an ion.
questions.modelAnswer: The m/z value is the mass of the ion divided by its charge, and for most singly charged ions it simply equals the ion's mass.

questions.stem: Explain why a singly charged ion of mass 12 and a doubly charged ion of mass 24 follow the same path in the spectrometer.
questions.modelAnswer: Both have identical m/z values of 12, and deflection in the magnetic field depends on that ratio rather than on mass or charge separately, so equal ratios give equal bending and equal detection positions.

questions.stem: A fragment ion of mass 28 appears twice in a spectrum, once singly charged and once doubly charged. Predict both m/z positions of this pair of peaks.
questions.modelAnswer: The singly charged ion lands at m/z 28 and the doubly charged version at m/z 14, because dividing the same mass by 1 and by 2 halves the ratio for the higher charge.

questions.stem: Chlorine exists as Cl-35 and Cl-37. What does a mass spectrum of a chlorine-containing molecular ion show?

options.text: A single peak split evenly at exactly half height each
options.explanation: The 75:25 abundance ratio is not an even split.

options.text: Two molecular-ion peaks two units apart, in a 75 to 25 height ratio
options.explanation: The two isotopes give ions two mass units apart with heights matching their natural abundances.

options.text: One peak, because isotopes have identical mass
options.explanation: Isotopes differ in neutrons and therefore in mass, so two peaks appear.

options.text: Two peaks one unit apart in equal heights
options.explanation: The mass gap is two units and the heights are unequal.

questions.stem: The [M+1] peak in a mass spectrum is caused by

options.text: Hydrogen atoms adding mass during ionisation
options.explanation: No hydrogen is added during ionisation; the ion loses an electron only.

options.text: Double ionisation of some molecules
options.explanation: Double charging lowers m/z; it does not create an M+1 peak.

options.text: The natural abundance of carbon-13, about one atom in a hundred
options.explanation: One C-13 in the ion raises its mass by one unit, creating the satellite peak.

options.text: Fragment ions one unit lighter than the molecular ion
options.explanation: Fragments are smaller than the molecular ion, not one unit heavier.

questions.stem: Why is the M+1 peak of a hexane ion taller than that of an ethane ion?

options.text: Hexane molecules are more abundant in the sample
options.explanation: Abundance of the sample does not set the M+1 ratio within a molecule.

options.text: Ethane ions fragment before the M+1 can form
options.explanation: Fragmentation competes but does not suppress the isotope satellite systematically.

options.text: Hexane contains more hydrogen atoms that absorb charge
options.explanation: Hydrogen count does not drive the M+1 peak.

options.text: Hexane has six carbon atoms to ethane's two, so it has more chances to include a C-13
options.explanation: Each carbon contributes roughly a one-percent C-13 chance, so the satellite grows with carbon count.

questions.stem: Which peak gives the molecular mass of an unknown compound?

options.text: The top-m/z peak, the molecular ion
options.explanation: The intact ionised molecule carries the full molecular mass at the top of the m/z range.

options.text: The base peak, wherever it sits
options.explanation: The base peak is an abundance champion, often a fragment.

options.text: The peak at m/z 18 in every spectrum
options.explanation: 18 belongs to water-loss fragments in some compounds, not a universal marker.

options.text: The M+1 satellite peak
options.explanation: The M+1 peak is one unit above the molecular ion and is not the mass itself.

questions.stem: A molecular ion peak sits at m/z 70 and a small peak appears at m/z 71. The best reading is

options.text: A doubly charged ion and a singly charged one
options.explanation: Doubling charge halves m/z; it does not create a one-unit-up pair.

options.text: Molecular mass 70, with the 71 peak a carbon-13 satellite
options.explanation: The highest ordinary peak is the molecular ion; the small M+1 shoulder is the C-13 satellite.

options.text: Molecular mass 71, the larger value
options.explanation: The M+1 peak is not the molecular ion; it is the isotope variant.

options.text: Two different compounds mixed in the sample
options.explanation: An M and M+1 pair is the normal isotope signature of one compound.

questions.stem: State the relative abundances of the two main chlorine isotopes.
questions.modelAnswer: Chlorine-35 accounts for about 75 percent of chlorine atoms and chlorine-37 for about 25 percent.

questions.stem: Define relative abundance of an isotope.
questions.modelAnswer: Relative abundance is the proportion of one particular isotope within a natural mixture of the isotopes of that element.

questions.stem: Explain how mass spectrometry measures the relative abundances of boron's isotopes.
questions.modelAnswer: The spectrometer separates the boron-10 and boron-11 ions by their different masses, and the heights of the two peaks record how many of each ion arrived, which is the experimental relative abundance.

questions.stem: An ion of an element shows peaks at m/z 27 and m/z 18 for masses 54 and 36 at equal abundance. Identify the charge states and which ion deflects more.
questions.modelAnswer: The mass-54 ion is doubly charged (54/2 = 27) and the mass-36 ion is doubly charged (36/2 = 18); the m/z 18 ion deflects more because its smaller ratio bends further in the same magnetic field.

questions.stem: A peak at m/z 29 in an alkane spectrum most likely corresponds to which fragment?

options.text: A propyl cation C3H7+
options.explanation: Propyl sums to 43 mass units.

options.text: A water-loss peak
options.explanation: Water loss creates a peak 18 below a parent, not a standalone 29.

options.text: The ethyl cation C2H5+
options.explanation: Two carbons plus five hydrogens sum to 29 mass units, the classic ethyl cation.

options.text: The methyl cation CH3+
options.explanation: The methyl cation lands at 15, not 29.

questions.stem: Alkanes fragment in the mass spectrometer mainly by

options.text: Losing water molecules one after another
options.explanation: Alkanes carry no hydroxyl groups, so water loss is not their pathway.

options.text: Losing halogen atoms from the chain
options.explanation: Alkanes contain no halogens to lose.

options.text: Absorbing extra electrons until they split
options.explanation: Electron gain does not drive fragmentation; bond breaking after ionisation does.

options.text: Breaking C-C bonds to give a series of alkyl cations
options.explanation: The carbon backbone snaps at C-C links, producing the alkyl cation ladder.

questions.stem: A peak at m/z 44 arising from loss of a small molecule indicates departure of

options.text: Carbon dioxide
options.explanation: CO2 has a molecular mass of 44, one of the classic small-molecule losses.

options.text: Water
options.explanation: Water loss registers 18 units below the parent.

options.text: Carbon monoxide
options.explanation: CO registers 28 units below the parent.

options.text: Methane
options.explanation: Methane loss would register 16 units below the parent.

questions.stem: Two isomers share the same molecular ion at m/z 72. Mass spectrometry distinguishes them by

options.text: Checking the M+1 peak heights only
options.explanation: Same formula means the same carbon count, so M+1 heights match too.

options.text: Comparing their different fragment ion patterns
options.explanation: Isomers break at different bonds, so their fragment ladders differ even when the molecular mass matches.

options.text: Measuring their different molecular masses
options.explanation: The molecular masses are identical by assumption; fragments do the discriminating.

options.text: Counting their base peaks
options.explanation: Both spectra have one base peak each; the count is uninformative.

questions.stem: A fragment table lists C3H7+ at m/z 43. A spectrum showing strong peaks at 29 and 43 but weak 57 suggests the chain

options.text: Cannot be an alkane
options.explanation: Alkyl cations are exactly what alkanes produce.

options.text: Has lost all its hydrogen atoms
options.explanation: Hydrogen retention is visible in the alkyl formulas matching the peaks.

options.text: Contains ethyl and propyl segments but little or no butyl-length straight run
options.explanation: The observed cations map to chain pieces of two and three carbons, with little four-carbon character.

options.text: Must be a four-carbon straight chain throughout
options.explanation: A butyl cation at 57 would then be strong, contradicting the weak 57 peak.

questions.stem: State the m/z values of the peaks formed by loss of water, carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide.
questions.modelAnswer: Losses of small molecules give peaks at 18 for water, 28 for carbon monoxide and 44 for carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: Define fragmentation in mass spectrometry.
questions.modelAnswer: Fragmentation is the breaking of the molecular ion into smaller ions, molecules and radicals, each charged piece appearing as its own peak.

questions.stem: Explain why fragmentation patterns add structural information beyond the molecular ion peak.
questions.modelAnswer: The molecular ion only reports total mass, while fragments reveal which bonded pieces the molecule contains, so two isomers of equal mass produce different fragment sets that pin down the arrangement of atoms.

questions.stem: A spectrum of a hydrocarbon shows molecular ion 58 and strong peaks at 43 and 29. Suggest which straight-chain alkane fits and justify the fragment assignments.
questions.modelAnswer: Butane fits: molecular ion 58 matches C4H10, the 43 peak is the propyl cation C3H7+ from losing a methyl radical, and the 29 peak is the ethyl cation C2H5+ from losing two carbons.

questions.stem: Why does a halogenoalkane spectrum show multiple peaks around the molecular ion?

options.text: The carbon chain breaks at many positions at once
options.explanation: Chain fragmentation gives fragment peaks, not the molecular-ion cluster.

options.text: The halogen atom carries variable charge
options.explanation: The halogen is part of a singly charged ion; charge does not vary here.

options.text: Water loss creates satellite peaks near the molecular ion
options.explanation: Water loss is the alcohol signature, not the halogenoalkane cause.

options.text: The halogen's isotopes create molecular ions of slightly different masses
options.explanation: Each isotopic version of the molecule ionises, giving a cluster of peaks spanning a few mass units.

questions.stem: The mass spectrum of CH3Br shows two molecular-ion peaks at m/z 94 and 96 of about equal height. This reveals

options.text: Bromine's two main isotopes occur in nearly equal proportions, 79Br and 81Br
options.explanation: Equal peak heights at two units apart are the 50:50 bromine isotope signature.

options.text: The sample contains two different brominated compounds
options.explanation: One compound explains both peaks through its isotope mixture.

options.text: The molecular ion has lost a hydrogen between the peaks
options.explanation: The two-unit gap is isotope mass, not hydrogen loss.

options.text: Chlorine contamination doubles every peak
options.explanation: The two-unit equal pair is bromine's signature; chlorine gives a 75:25 three-unit pair.

questions.stem: An alcohol spectrum shows a peak 18 units below the molecular ion. Which loss explains it?

options.text: Loss of ethene
options.explanation: Ethene loss would drop 28 units.

options.text: Loss of a water molecule from the molecular ion
options.explanation: Alcohols readily eliminate water, shifting the fragment 18 units down.

options.text: Loss of an oxygen atom only
options.explanation: Losing just O would drop 16 units.

options.text: Loss of a hydroxyl group plus nothing else
options.explanation: Losing OH alone drops 17 units; the 18 gap is the full water molecule.

questions.stem: Which fragment, characteristic of alcohols, sits at m/z 31?

options.text: C3H7+
options.explanation: Propyl sits at 43.

options.text: OH+
options.explanation: The bare hydroxyl cation sums to 17.

options.text: CH2OH+
options.explanation: The hydroxymethyl cation sums to 31 and marks an alcohol's oxygen end.

options.text: C2H5+
options.explanation: The ethyl cation sits at 29 and is not alcohol-specific.

questions.stem: Propan-1-ol shows a peak at m/z 42. Which fragmentation produces it?

options.text: Loss of a hydrogen radical
options.explanation: Losing H gives the 59 peak of C3H7O+.

options.text: Loss of a CH2OH radical
options.explanation: That loss gives the 29 peak of C2H5+.

options.text: Loss of an ethyl radical
options.explanation: That loss gives the 31 peak of CH2OH+.

options.text: Loss of a water molecule from the molecular ion
options.explanation: Propan-1-ol minus water is C3H6+, whose mass is 42.

questions.stem: State the two most useful diagnostic peaks in an alcohol mass spectrum.
questions.modelAnswer: A peak 18 below the molecular ion from water loss, and the CH2OH+ fragment at m/z 31.

questions.stem: State the three precipitate-colour clues... in fact, state how halogenoalkane spectra reveal their halogen.
questions.modelAnswer: The molecular ion appears as a cluster of peaks whose spacing and height ratio match the halogen's isotope pattern, such as the equal pair two units apart for bromine.

questions.stem: Explain why the two molecular-ion peaks of bromomethane have equal heights.
questions.modelAnswer: Bromine-79 and bromine-81 exist in nearly equal natural proportions, so almost exactly half the bromomethane molecules carry each isotope and the two molecular-ion peaks rise to nearly equal heights.

questions.stem: An unknown alcohol shows peaks at 60 (molecular ion), 42, 31 and 29. Identify the compound and assign each fragment.
questions.modelAnswer: Propan-1-ol: molecular ion C3H8O+ at 60, water loss gives C3H6+ at 42, loss of an ethyl radical gives CH2OH+ at 31, and loss of the CH2OH radical gives C2H5+ at 29.
